title: NSW HSC Physics Module 5: Advanced Mechanics
description: A classroom review of the three Module 5 inquiry questions: projectile models, circular motion, and the gravitational motion of planets and satellites.
course: NSW HSC Physics — Module 5: Advanced Mechanics
author: Generated with Classroom Jeopardy Quiz Maker

questions.prompt: In the standard projectile-motion model near Earth, what are the horizontal and vertical accelerations?
questions.answer: Horizontal: 0 m s⁻². Vertical: 9.8 m s⁻² downward (−9.8 m s⁻² if upward is positive).

questions.prompt: A ball is launched at 20 m s⁻¹, 30° above horizontal. Resolve its initial velocity into horizontal and vertical components.
questions.answer: Horizontal: 20 cos 30° = 17.3 m s⁻¹. Vertical: 20 sin 30° = 10.0 m s⁻¹ upward.

questions.prompt: At the highest point B, identify arrows P and Q as the projectile’s velocity and acceleration.
questions.answer: P is velocity, horizontally tangent to the path. Q is acceleration, vertically downward.
questions.imageAlt: A parabolic projectile path with point B at the apex. Arrow P points horizontally right and arrow Q points vertically down.

questions.prompt: A projectile is launched horizontally at 12 m s⁻¹ from a 45 m cliff. Using g = 9.8 m s⁻², how far from the cliff does it land?
questions.answer: Time to fall = √(2h/g) = 3.03 s; horizontal range = 12 × 3.03 = 36.4 m.

questions.prompt: A projectile is launched from level ground at 25 m s⁻¹ and 40°. It lands at the same height. Using g = 9.8 m s⁻², find its range.
The graph models range against launch angle for a fixed speed and equal launch and landing heights. Which two marked angles give equal range, and why?
questions.answer: 30° and 60°. They are complementary angles, so sin(2θ) has the same value.
questions.imageAlt: A graph of relative projectile range against launch angle. The curve peaks at 45 degrees, while points at 30 and 60 degrees have equal height.

questions.prompt: A projectile leaves a 20 m cliff at 30 m s⁻¹, 35° above horizontal. Using g = 9.8 m s⁻² and no air resistance, find its horizontal range.
questions.answer: Vertical motion gives t = 4.43 s. Horizontal speed = 30 cos 35° = 24.6 m s⁻¹, so range = 24.6 × 4.43 = 109 m (approximately).

questions.prompt: In uniform circular motion, in which direction do the acceleration and net force point?
questions.answer: Towards the centre of the circle: the centripetal direction.

questions.prompt: An object moves at 10 m s⁻¹ in a circle of radius 5.0 m. What is its centripetal acceleration?
questions.answer: a_c = v²/r = 10²/5.0 = 20 m s⁻² towards the centre.

questions.prompt: The object is at the right-hand side of the circle and moving anticlockwise. Identify arrows P and Q.
questions.answer: P is the instantaneous velocity, tangent and upward. Q is the centripetal acceleration or net force, directed left towards the centre.
questions.imageAlt: A circular path with an object at the right-hand side. Arrow P points upward tangentially and arrow Q points left towards the centre.

questions.prompt: A 1200 kg car travels at 20 m s⁻¹ around a level curve of radius 50 m. What net horizontal force is required?
questions.answer: F_c = mv²/r = 1200 × 20²/50 = 9.60 × 10³ N towards the centre.

questions.prompt: A frictionless banked track has radius 80 m and design speed 22 m s⁻¹. Using g = 9.8 m s⁻², calculate the bank angle θ.
questions.imageAlt: A car on a banked road inclined at angle theta, with weight vertically down and the normal force perpendicular to the road.

questions.prompt: A 500 kg roller-coaster car passes the top of a vertical loop of radius 12 m at 15 m s⁻¹. Calculate the track’s normal force on the car.
questions.answer: At the top, mg + N = mv²/r. Therefore N = 500(15²/12 − 9.8) = 4.48 × 10³ N downward, towards the centre.
questions.imageAlt: A roller-coaster car at the top of a vertical loop. Its weight and the track's normal force both point downward towards the loop centre.

questions.prompt: A 0.25 kg stopper moves in a horizontal circle of radius 0.80 m, completing 15 revolutions in 12 s. Find the centripetal force.
questions.answer: Period = 12/15 = 0.80 s; v = 2πr/T = 6.28 m s⁻¹; F_c = mv²/r = 12.3 N.

questions.prompt: State Newton’s law of universal gravitation.
questions.answer: F = Gm₁m₂/r². The attractive force acts along the line joining the two masses.

questions.prompt: A planet’s gravitational field strength is g at distance R from its centre. What is the field strength at distance 2R?
questions.answer: g/4, because gravitational field strength follows an inverse-square relationship.

questions.prompt: A planet follows the elliptical orbit shown. At which labelled point is it moving fastest, and which law supports this?
questions.answer: At P, perihelion. Kepler’s second law: equal areas are swept out in equal times, so the planet moves faster when closer to the Sun.
questions.imageAlt: An elliptical orbit with the Sun at the left focus. Point P is close to the Sun at perihelion and point A is far away at aphelion.

questions.prompt: Find the speed of a circular Earth satellite at orbital radius 7.0 × 10⁶ m. Use G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ and Earth’s mass 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg.
questions.answer: v = √(GM/r) = 7.54 × 10³ m s⁻¹, or 7.54 km s⁻¹.

questions.prompt: Calculate Earth’s escape speed from the surface. Use G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹, M = 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg and R = 6.37 × 10⁶ m.
questions.answer: v_e = √(2GM/R) = 1.12 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹, or about 11.2 km s⁻¹.

questions.prompt: Give the three orbital requirements for a satellite to remain geostationary above one point on Earth.
questions.answer: It must have a 24-hour sidereal period, orbit above the equator, and move in the same direction as Earth’s rotation.

questions.prompt: A satellite has a 12.0 h circular orbit around a planet of mass 6.0 × 10²⁴ kg. Find the orbital radius. Use G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹.
questions.answer: r = [GMT²/(4π²)]^(1/3) = 2.66 × 10⁷ m from the planet’s centre.

finalRound.prompt: A spacecraft in a circular orbit makes a brief tangential prograde burn at point X, then coasts. Describe the new orbit and identify where its perigee and apogee occur.
finalRound.answer: The spacecraft enters an elliptical orbit. Point X is the perigee, and the apogee is on the opposite side; the prograde burn raises the far side of the orbit.
finalRound.imageAlt: A spacecraft at point X on a circular orbit around Earth, with an arrow tangent to the orbit showing a prograde engine burn.
